entries.title: Derivative
entries.definition: The derivative of f(x) measures its instantaneous rate of change with respect to x. The engine computes symbolic derivatives via calc:diff, and supports partial, mixed-partial, and higher-order derivatives through calc:partial, calc:partial_mixed, and repeated calc:diff calls.

entries.title: Integral
entries.definition: An indefinite integral (antiderivative) or definite integral computes the accumulated area under f(x). The engine supports indefinite (calc:integrate), definite (calc:definite_int), double (calc:double_int), triple (calc:triple_int), and polar (calc:polar_int) integrals, plus numerical integration via calc:numerical_int.

entries.title: Taylor Series
entries.definition: A Taylor series approximates a function near a point using a polynomial built from its derivatives at that point. The engine's calc:taylor op takes an expression, a center point, and an order (number of terms).

entries.title: Limit
entries.definition: A limit describes the value a function approaches as its input approaches some point (or infinity). The engine supports two-sided, left-hand, right-hand, and limits at +/- infinity via calc:limit, calc:limit_left, calc:limit_right, calc:limit_inf, and calc:limit_neginf.

entries.title: Determinant
entries.definition: The determinant of a square matrix is a scalar that describes how the matrix scales volume, and whether it's invertible (a zero determinant means the matrix is singular). Computed via la:determinant.

entries.title: Matrix Inverse
entries.definition: The inverse of a square matrix A, written A^-1, satisfies A*A^-1 = I. A matrix is invertible only if its determinant is nonzero (i.e. it's non-singular). Computed via la:inverse.

entries.title: Eigenvalues & Eigenvectors
entries.definition: An eigenvector v of a matrix A satisfies A*v = lambda*v for some scalar lambda (its eigenvalue) — v's direction is unchanged by the transformation. Computed via la:eigen_full (both) or la:eigenvalues/la:eigenvectors (separately).

entries.title: Singular Matrix
entries.definition: A matrix is singular if its determinant is zero, meaning it has no inverse and its rows/columns are linearly dependent. Check with la:determinant (zero result) or la:rank (rank less than the matrix's dimension).

entries.title: Mean
entries.definition: The arithmetic mean (average) of a dataset is the sum of its values divided by the count. Computed via stat:mean.

entries.title: Standard Deviation
entries.definition: Standard deviation measures how spread out a dataset's values are around the mean — the square root of the variance. Computed via stat:stddev (variance via stat:variance).

entries.title: Correlation (Pearson)
entries.definition: The Pearson correlation coefficient measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two variables, ranging from -1 (perfect negative) to +1 (perfect positive). Computed via stat:pearson.

entries.title: Linear Regression
entries.definition: Linear regression fits a straight line (y = mx + b) that best predicts y from x by minimizing squared error. Computed via stat:linear_reg; polynomial regression is available via stat:poly_reg.

entries.title: Hypothesis Testing
entries.definition: A hypothesis test checks whether observed data is consistent with a claim (the null hypothesis), producing a p-value/test statistic. The engine supports one- and two-sample t-tests, z-tests, chi-square tests, ANOVA, and many nonparametric tests (Wilcoxon, Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis).

entries.title: Greatest Common Divisor (GCD)
entries.definition: The GCD of two integers is the largest integer that divides both without a remainder. Computed via nt:gcd; the extended version (which also returns Bezout coefficients) is nt:extended_gcd.

entries.title: Prime Factorization
entries.definition: Prime factorization decomposes an integer into a product of prime numbers. Computed via nt:prime_factors; related checks include nt:is_prime and nt:divisors.

entries.title: Modular Arithmetic
entries.definition: Modular arithmetic works with remainders after division by a fixed modulus. The engine supports modular exponentiation (nt:mod_pow), modular inverses (nt:mod_inverse), and linear/quadratic congruences (nt:linear_cong, nt:quad_cong).

entries.title: Combinations & Permutations
entries.definition: Combinations (nCr) count ways to choose r items from n without regard to order; permutations (nPr) count ordered arrangements. Computed via dm:combinations and dm:permutations.

entries.title: Shortest Path (Dijkstra)
entries.definition: Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest path from a source node to all others in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights, given as an adjacency matrix. Computed via dm:dijkstra (all-pairs version: dm:floyd_warshall).

entries.title: Distance Formula
entries.definition: The distance between two points is the length of the straight line connecting them: sqrt((x2-x1)^2 + (y2-y1)^2) in 2D, extended with a z-term in 3D. Computed via geo:distance_2d / geo:distance_3d.

entries.title: Complex Roots
entries.definition: Every nonzero complex number has exactly n distinct nth roots, evenly spaced around a circle in the complex plane. Computed via ca:all_roots.

entries.title: Residue (Complex Analysis)
entries.definition: The residue of a function at a pole is the coefficient of the 1/(z-z0) term in its Laurent series there, central to evaluating contour integrals via the residue theorem. Computed via ca:residue.

entries.title: Newton's Method
entries.definition: Newton's method finds roots of f(x) by iterating x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n), converging quickly from a good starting guess. Computed via na:newton; bisection (na:bisection) and the secant method (na:secant) are more robust alternatives.

entries.title: Runge-Kutta (RK4)
entries.definition: RK4 numerically solves an ODE dy/dt = f(t,y) by taking weighted steps using four slope estimates per interval, far more accurate than Euler's method for the same step size. Computed via de:rk4 (also available: de:euler, de:rk2, de:rk45, de:adams_bashforth).

entries.title: Laplace Transform
entries.definition: The Laplace transform converts a function of time into a function of a complex frequency variable s, turning differential equations into algebraic ones. Computed via de:laplace (inverse: de:inverse_laplace).

entries.title: Groups (Abstract Algebra)
entries.definition: A group is a set with an operation satisfying closure, associativity, identity, and inverses. The engine can build cyclic groups (aa:cyclic), symmetric groups (aa:symmetric), and dihedral groups (aa:dihedral), and check properties like abelian-ness (aa:is_abelian).

entries.title: Bayes' Theorem
entries.definition: Bayes' theorem relates conditional probabilities: P(A|B) = P(B|A)*P(A) / P(B), updating a prior belief given new evidence. Computed via stat:bayes.

entries.title: Markov Chain
entries.definition: A Markov chain models a system that moves between states with transition probabilities depending only on the current state. Its steady-state distribution (if it exists) is computed via stat:markov_steady.

entries.title: Central Limit Theorem
entries.definition: The Central Limit Theorem states that the sampling distribution of the mean of many independent samples approaches a normal distribution, regardless of the population's original distribution, as sample size grows. Demonstrated via stat:clt_demo.

entries.title: Logistic Growth
entries.definition: Logistic growth models population growth that slows as it approaches a carrying capacity K, following dN/dt = r*N*(1-N/K). Computed via am:logistic_growth.

entries.title: SIR Epidemic Model
entries.definition: The SIR model divides a population into Susceptible, Infected, and Recovered compartments and tracks how they evolve over time given transmission (beta) and recovery (gamma) rates. Computed via am:sir; the reproduction number R0 = beta/gamma is available via am:reproduction_number.

entries.title: Expression Syntax
entries.definition: Plain expressions (e.g. "2^8 + sqrt(16)") are parsed directly by the engine. Structured operations use either shorthand like "diff[x^2,x]" (expanded by Preprocessor.cpp) or the raw wire format "prefix:op|payload" (e.g. "la:determinant|[[1,2],[3,4]]", "stat:mean|{\"x\":[1,2,3]}"), where payload is either a bracketed literal (Linear Algebra) or a JSON object (most other modules).
entries.syntax: See chatbot/README.md 'Command format reference' for the full breakdown.
